items.stem: An answer cites an entire 50-page document for a single specific figure. Why is this poor citation design?

options.text: It does not let a reader locate the passage that actually supports the figure
options.rationale: Correct: a useful citation points to the specific supporting span, not the whole document.

options.text: Documents may not be cited at all
options.rationale: Documents can be cited; the issue is granularity.
Format is not the problem here.

options.text: Fifty pages is too short to cite
options.rationale: Length is not the issue; precision is.

items.explanation: Correct: a useful citation points to the specific supporting span, not the whole document.

items.stem: Which TWO are needed for citations to resolve back to source? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Chunks that carry a source reference and offset/location
options.rationale: Correct: provenance metadata lets a citation resolve to a passage.

options.text: Preserving that metadata through the chunking pipeline
options.rationale: Correct: if metadata is dropped during chunking, citations cannot resolve.

options.text: Discarding chunk IDs to save space
Relying only on the answer text with no metadata
options.rationale: Answer text alone cannot be traced to a source.

items.explanation: Correct: provenance metadata lets a citation resolve to a passage.

items.stem: A claim carries a citation, but opening the cited span shows it does not support the claim. What does this reveal?

options.text: A citation's presence does not guarantee the claim is supported; evidence must be checked
options.rationale: Correct: attribution accuracy must be verified, not assumed from a citation's existence.

options.text: The claim is automatically correct because it is cited
options.rationale: Presence of a citation is not proof of support.
They can point to non-supporting content.
The fix is to correct attribution, not delete sources.
